pos: n. (proper name; one of David's thirty mighty men, the Hushathite, also called Sibbecai)
etymology: Hebrew Mebunnay, of uncertain derivation, perhaps built up, from banah, to build; the same man is called Sibbecai in the Chronicles.
biblical_def: Mebunnai is one of David's thirty, named in the roll at the end of Second Samuel: “Abiezer the Anethothite, Mebunnai the Hushathite” (2 Samuel 23:27). The list is a careful piece of record-keeping, beginning with the men nearest the king: “Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem” (2 Samuel 23:24), and closing with a name that should make a reader stop: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). The parallel roll in Chronicles calls the same Hushathite Sibbecai: “Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite” (1 Chronicles 11:29), and the margin of the Authorized Version notes the two names as one man. Under the name Sibbechai he is credited with killing a Philistine giant at Gezer. Mebunnai is therefore a man with two names, a town for his surname, one slain giant, and a place on the honour roll of a king — and he is listed four names above the man David murdered. God keeps both facts in the same chapter.

corruption_summary: Honour rolls are used to flatter the leader; David's list of mighty men ends with the name of the man he had killed.
corruption_paragraphs: An official roll of honour normally serves the man at the top. David's does not. It names Mebunnai and the rest, and then it names Uriah the Hittite — the soldier whose wife David took and whose death he arranged — and counts him among the thirty and seven. The Spirit of God did not let the record be cleaned up.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture tells the truth about its heroes, that faithful service is remembered by name, and that a king's sin is not erased from the register of the men he led.

pos: n. (proper name; a Philistine giant of Gath slain by Sibbechai, also called Saph)
etymology: Hebrew Sippay, of uncertain derivation; the same giant is called Saph in the parallel account in Second Samuel.
biblical_def: Sippai is one of the sons of the giant at Gath, killed in the wars that cleared the land after Goliath fell: “And it came to pass after this, that there arose war at Gezer with the Philistines; at which time Sibbechai the Hushathite slew Sippai, that was of the children of the giant: and they were subdued” (1 Chronicles 20:4). The parallel passage in Second Samuel calls him Saph, and the Authorized Version's margin notes the two forms as one man. The next verses of Chronicles finish the family. One brother fell to Elhanan, and another was a monstrosity of stature and count: “And yet again there was war at Gath, where was a man of great stature, whose fingers and toes were four and twenty, six on each hand, and six on each foot: and he also was the son of the giant” (1 Chronicles 20:6). Then the historian closes the account: “These were born unto the giant in Gath; and they fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants” (1 Chronicles 20:8), as Samuel had closed it too: “These four were born to the giant in Gath, and fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants” (2 Samuel 21:22). David killed the father; servants of David killed the sons.

corruption_paragraphs: The story most people know ends with a stone and a sling. Scripture carries it further: the giant had sons, and they came out of Gath again and again, and each had to be met and killed by one of David's men. A victory of faith does not exempt the next generation from the fighting.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Lord gives His people victory through ordinary servants after the great champion has gone first, and that an enemy's seed must be dealt with in its turn.

pos: n. (proper name; the brother of Goliath the Gittite, slain by Elhanan)
etymology: Hebrew Lachmi, perhaps from lechem, bread, or connected with Bethlehem; named once, at 1 Chronicles 20:5.
biblical_def: Lahmi is the brother of Goliath, and he is named once: “And there was war again with the Philistines; and Elhanan the son of Jair slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear staff was like a weaver's beam” (1 Chronicles 20:5). The detail of the spear staff is the mark of the family; the same phrase is used of Goliath himself, and it tells the reader that this was no lesser man than the champion of the valley of Elah. He belonged to a house of such men: “And it came to pass after this, that there arose war at Gezer with the Philistines; at which time Sibbechai the Hushathite slew Sippai, that was of the children of the giant: and they were subdued” (1 Chronicles 20:4); and another brother was stranger still: “And yet again there was war at Gath, where was a man of great stature, whose fingers and toes were four and twenty, six on each hand, and six on each foot: and he also was the son of the giant” (1 Chronicles 20:6). The chronicle sums the whole house: “These were born unto the giant in Gath; and they fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants” (1 Chronicles 20:8). A man whose name nobody remembers killed Goliath's brother.

pos: n. (proper name; the father of Achish king of Gath)
etymology: Hebrew Maok, perhaps oppression or pressed down, from muk, to be low; named once, at 1 Samuel 27:2.
biblical_def: Maoch is named once, and only as the father of the Philistine king with whom David took refuge. The flight is explained by David's own reasoning, and it is not his finest hour: “And David said in his heart, I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul: there is nothing better for me than that I should speedily escape into the land of the Philistines; and Saul shall despair of me, to seek me any more in any coast of Israel: so shall I escape out of his hand” (1 Samuel 27:1). So he went: “And David arose, and he passed over with the six hundred men that were with him unto Achish, the son of Maoch, king of Gath” (1 Samuel 27:2), and settled there with his household: “And David dwelt with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, even David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the Carmelitess, Nabal's wife” (1 Samuel 27:3). It was not the first time he had tried Gath: “And David arose, and fled that day for fear of Saul, and went to Achish the king of Gath” (1 Samuel 21:10) — on that occasion he escaped only by feigning madness. The anointed king of Israel spent sixteen months as a vassal in the city of Goliath, and God brought him out of it to a throne.

corruption_paragraphs: David's move to Gath was not faith. The text gives his motive in his own words — I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul — though God had anointed him and promised him the kingdom. He went to live under the father-in-law city of his old enemy, and it led him into a tangle he barely escaped. Scripture does not tidy it up.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps His promise to a man whose heart has gone to unbelieving calculation, and that a saint's worst reasoning is still recorded for the warning of the rest.

pos: n. (proper name; the fifth captain of David's monthly courses)
etymology: Hebrew Shamhuth, perhaps desolation or renown; called the Izrahite, and named once, at 1 Chronicles 27:8.
biblical_def: Shamhuth is the captain of the fifth of David's twelve monthly courses: “The fifth captain for the fifth month was Shamhuth the Izrahite: and in his course were twenty and four thousand” (1 Chronicles 27:8). The arrangement is described at the head of the chapter: “Now the children of Israel after their number, to wit, the chief fathers and captains of thousands and hundreds, and their officers that served the king in any matter of the courses, which came in and went out month by month throughout all the months of the year, of every course were twenty and four thousand” (1 Chronicles 27:1). Twelve divisions of twenty-four thousand men each, one on duty every month, so that the kingdom was always defended and no man was permanently under arms. The captains before and after Shamhuth are named: “The fourth captain for the fourth month was Asahel the brother of Joab, and Zebadiah his son after him: and in his course were twenty and four thousand” (1 Chronicles 27:7), and “The sixth captain for the sixth month was Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite: and in his course were twenty and four thousand” (1 Chronicles 27:9). This is not a poem; it is a duty roster, and it is in the Bible. God thought the shift schedule of Israel's army worth preserving.

The man who keeps the rota is serving as truly as the man who writes the psalm.

pos: n. (proper name; the fifth son of Jesse and a brother of David)
etymology: Hebrew Radday, perhaps the LORD subdues, from radah, to rule or subdue; named once, at 1 Chronicles 2:14.
biblical_def: Raddai is a brother of David, the fifth of the sons of Jesse, and he is named once in Scripture: “Nethaneel the fourth, Raddai the fifth” (1 Chronicles 2:14). The genealogy around him gives the whole house: “And Jesse begat his firstborn Eliab, and Abinadab the second, and Shimma the third” (1 Chronicles 2:13), and then “Ozem the sixth, David the seventh” (1 Chronicles 2:15). Raddai was in the house at Bethlehem on the day Samuel came with the horn of oil, and he was one of the sons made to pass before the prophet and refused: “Again, Jesse made seven of his sons to pass before Samuel. And Samuel said unto Jesse, The LORD hath not chosen these” (1 Samuel 16:10). Seven grown sons walked past a prophet and were all declined, and the youngest was fetched from the sheep. Raddai is the ordinary case of the man God passes over — not a wicked man, not a rejected man in the sense of judgment, simply not the chosen one. He had to live the rest of his life as the brother of the anointed, and Scripture keeps his name because the election of David was the non-election of six others in the same room.

corruption_summary: Divine choice is resented as unfairness; six of Jesse's sons were passed by in one afternoon and the Scripture keeps their names.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of election is commonly refused on the ground that it is unjust to those not chosen. First Samuel sixteen is the thing itself in a single room: seven sons, one prophet, one horn of oil, and the LORD hath not chosen these. Raddai was not wicked and not condemned; he was simply not the man God had named. The choosing belongs to God, and He gives no account of it to the family.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God chooses whom He will, that He looks on the heart and not on the outward appearance, and that the unchosen brother of a chosen man is still called to serve in his place.

pos: n. (proper name; the Hagerite who was over David's flocks)
etymology: Hebrew Yaziz, perhaps he shall make prominent, or from a root signifying to shine; named once, at 1 Chronicles 27:31.
biblical_def: Jaziz is the officer set over the king's flocks, and he is named once, at the end of a list of David's stewards: “And over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagerite. All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David's” (1 Chronicles 27:31). The men named with him had the rest of the royal property in charge: “And over the herds that fed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite: and over the herds that were in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai” (1 Chronicles 27:29), and “Over the camels also was Obil the Ishmaelite: and over the asses was Jehdeiah the Meronothite” (1 Chronicles 27:30). Immediately after the stewards come the men of counsel: “Also Jonathan David's uncle was a counsellor, a wise man, and a scribe: and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni was with the king's sons” (1 Chronicles 27:32). Two things in this short list are worth a reader's attention. First, a shepherd king kept a man over the flocks and wrote his name down. Second, Jaziz was a Hagerite, and Obil an Ishmaelite — foreigners trusted with the king's own substance, in charge of the animals their own nations best understood.

pos: n. (proper name; the father of Jashobeam, and an overseer in Nehemiah's Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Zabdi'el, God has given or my gift is God, from zabad, to bestow, and 'el, God.
biblical_def: Zabdiel is the name of two men, separated by five centuries, both of whom stood near the head of an ordered company. The first is the father of David's first captain: “Over the first course for the first month was Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel: and in his course were twenty and four thousand” (1 Chronicles 27:2). That course belonged to the system described in the verse before it: “Now the children of Israel after their number, to wit, the chief fathers and captains of thousands and hundreds, and their officers that served the king in any matter of the courses, which came in and went out month by month throughout all the months of the year, of every course were twenty and four thousand” (1 Chronicles 27:1). The second Zabdiel is an overseer in the rebuilt city: “And their brethren, mighty men of valour, an hundred twenty and eight: and their overseer was Zabdiel, the son of one of the great men” (Nehemiah 11:14). He is listed among the priests settled in Jerusalem, immediately after the men who did the work of the house: “And their brethren that did the work of the house were eight hundred twenty and two” (Nehemiah 11:12). The name means God has given, and in both cases it is attached to a man set over others for service.

corruption_paragraphs: Both men who bear this name stand over others — one fathering the captain of the first course, one overseeing a hundred twenty-eight men of valour — and the name they carry says God has given. An office is a gift held in trust, not a possession earned, and Hebrew parents put that confession into their children's names.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every capacity for leadership is bestowed, that overseers in the house of God are appointed and not self-raised, and that order among the people of God is part of their health.

pos: n. (proper name; one of David's mighty men, the Ahohite, also called Zalmon)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ilay, of uncertain derivation, perhaps exalted; called the Ahohite, and named once under this form, at 1 Chronicles 11:29.
biblical_def: Ilai is one of David's valiant men, named in the Chronicles' roll: “Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite” (1 Chronicles 11:29). The parallel list in Second Samuel gives the same man at the same place in the order under another name: “Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite” (2 Samuel 23:28), and the margin of the Authorized Version notes the two as one. The names before and after him locate him in the company: “Also the valiant men of the armies were, Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem” (1 Chronicles 11:26), and “Maharai the Netophathite, Heled the son of Baanah the Netophathite” (1 Chronicles 11:30). Ahohite was the family name of several of David's best soldiers, Dodo and Eleazar among them. Of Ilai himself nothing is told but the fact of his valour and his house. Two of the four lists of David's men give him different names, which has fed the charge that the registers are corrupt; the plain answer is that Hebrew men commonly bore two names, and the Chronicler knew which company he was describing.

corruption_summary: Double names in the registers are read as textual error; a man with two names is not two men, nor a mistake.
corruption_paragraphs: It is urged against the historical books that their lists disagree — Ilai here, Zalmon there, Mebunnai for Sibbecai, Saph for Sippai. The objection assumes that a man may have only one name, which was never the custom in Israel or anywhere in the ancient east. The Authorized Version's own margins note the equivalences, and the order of the names in the two rolls confirms them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the trustworthiness of Scripture's registers read according to their own conventions, and the honour God gives to valiant men whose deeds He does not describe.

pos: n. (proper name; one who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah)
etymology: Hebrew Shobeq, perhaps forsaking or one who leaves off; named once, at Nehemiah 10:24.
biblical_def: Shobek is one of the chiefs of the people who put their seal to the covenant Nehemiah drew up after the reading of the law. His name stands in a bare list of three: “Hallohesh, Pileha, Shobek” (Nehemiah 10:24). The document begins with the governor himself: “Now those that sealed were, Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah, and Zidkijah” (Nehemiah 10:1), and it is joined not only by the signatories but by the whole congregation: “And the rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the porters, the singers, the Nethinims, and all they that had separated themselves from the people of the lands unto the law of God, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, every one having knowledge, and having understanding” (Nehemiah 10:28). What they bound themselves to is stated without any softening: “They clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God's law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes” (Nehemiah 10:29). Shobek signed a curse against himself if he should not obey. That is what a covenant was.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Shobek is a Hebrew proper name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.
webster_full: Shobek is a Hebrew proper name; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

corruption_summary: Commitment is kept deliberately vague; the men of Nehemiah's day signed their names to a curse and an oath to obey God's law.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religion prefers an unspecified sincerity to a stated obligation, so that nothing can ever be said to have been broken. Nehemiah's generation wrote the obligation down, named the law they would keep, and sealed the document with their own names under a curse. Shobek is in that list.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that covenant with God is definite, public and binding, that the whole household joined it, and that those who entered it did so with understanding.
